content.title: 2024 Housing Needs Assessment Findings
content.summary: Arvada's housing inventory is predominantly composed of detached single-family homes, with 71% of units falling into this category, leading to a median sales price of $606,000 that is unaffordable for many residents. The city needs to add approximately 2,790 affordable rental units for low-income renters, and only 6% of for-sale homes are within reach for renters transitioning to homeownership. Community feedback indicates a strong desire for increased investment in affordable housing options, particularly for low- to middle-income workers.
content.body:
## Inventory

Arvada’s physical housing inventory is woefully lacking in a diversity of home types that could produce natural affordability for both renters and potential homebuyers. Nearly 2/3 (71%) of all housing units in Arvada are detached, single-family homes. The median sales price for a single-family home in Arvada was $606,000 as of the end of 2023, meaning a household would need to earn $199,000 a year to afford it. An analysis of Arvada’s housing stock and available inventory, when compared to resident incomes, revealed that:

- For renters earning less than 50% AMI, the City would have to add an additional 2,790 units at an affordable rent so that tenants were not spending more than 30% of their income on housing.
- Only 6% of the for-sale housing stock would be within the budget of renters looking to transition into homeownership; those earning between 50%-120% AMI (38% of all renters) and looking to transition into homeownership, only 6% of the for-sale housing stock would be within their budget.

### Challenges

Due to the lack of rental inventory and low stock of lower priced for-sale homes, many of Arvada’s local workers have nowhere to live within the City. There is no industry in Arvada that on average, pays a high enough salary to purchase a home at the median sales price. Only eight industries pay a high enough average salary for employees to rent an apartment in Arvada without being cost burdened.

## Administrative Burden

Interviews with developers and other stakeholders revealed a sentiment that the City was placing a development burden on projects that would be attainable and affordable for low- to moderate-income workers. There was a specific request for a more expedited review process, as well as the inclusion of some development incentives to be added to the Land Use Development Code, such as height or density bonuses, where appropriate.

*Note*: As a condition of opting in to Proposition 123, the City of Arvada must create a plan for a 90-day review process for residential affordable development by Dec. 31, 2026.

## Community Input

As a component of the assessment, Root Policy Research distributed a comprehensive community survey for both in-commuters to Arvada and local Arvada residents. The survey found:

- 62% of in-commuters considered living in Arvada but were unable to find an acceptable home to either buy or rent in their price range
- 60% of all respondents believed the City should invest in housing stock for low- to middle-income wage workers
- Nearly half of Arvada residents believe that multi-family homes would be appropriate in their neighborhood. More believe that it could be appropriate elsewhere in Arvada.
